author: David Fideler
title: Jesus Christ, Sun of God: Ancient Cosmology and Early Christian Symbolism
source: gnosis.study scan, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-10
note: Gematria of the 888, the hexagon and the cube; the source of the second 888 video.
annotation: Fideler reads the early Christian symbols (the 888 of Iesous, the 153 fishes, the vesica) as survivals of Pythagorean number cosmology and Greek gematria, with the geometrical constructions drawn out. Used for the 888 video: the hexagon, the cube down its diagonal with eight corners, the Greek gematria table.

author: Frances A. Yates
title: The Art of Memory
bibnote: Reprinted as Frances Yates, Selected Works, vol. III, Routledge, London and New York, 1999
note: Simonides to Bruno and Camillo's theatre; the memory palace as a technology of the self.
annotation: The history of the classical art of memory (places and images, from Simonides and the Ad Herennium through Metrodorus's zodiac) into its medieval, Renaissance and Hermetic transformations: Camillo's Memory Theatre, Lull's wheels, Bruno's Shadows and Seals, Fludd's theatre and the Globe, ending with Leibniz. Read for the symbols repo's memoria catalogue (every system she presents, 176 reader entries merged into dossier-sized systems) and for the zodiac story video's Simonides opening.

author: Gustave Flaubert
title: The Temptation of St. Anthony
publisher: English translation, edition and translator not identified from the scan
bibnote: Internet Archive, University of Toronto copy (temptationofstan00flauuoft); French original La Tentation de saint Antoine, 1874
source: Internet Archive scan, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-12
note: La Tentation de saint Antoine, the 1874 final version; the scan has no OCR text layer.
annotation: Flaubert's closet drama of the hermit's night in the desert: the Queen of Sheba, the heresiarchs, the gods passing in procession, Hilarion, the Sphinx and the Chimera, and the last vision of matter. The 1874 version is the third; the scan is an early English translation whose translator the copy does not name.

author: Antonin Artaud; edited by Susan Sontag, translated by Helen Weaver
title: Selected Writings
bibnote: University of California Press reprint 1988, ISBN 0520064437
source: dokumen.pub scan, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-12
note: Theatre of Cruelty, the Tarahumara journey, the Rodez letters; Sontag's introduction.
annotation: Sontag's selection across Artaud's whole life: the correspondence with Rivière, the Surrealist texts, The Theatre and Its Double, the Mexican and Tarahumara writings, the Rodez letters and the late radio work, with her long introduction on Artaud as the exemplary case of the modern writer who fails at making a work and succeeds at making a life into one.

author: St. Bonaventure; translated by the author of 'The Life of S. Teresa' (Elizabeth Lockhart), preface by Henry Edward Manning
title: The Life of St. Francis of Assisi (Legenda maior)
bibnote: Google Books scan; preface by Henry Edward Manning; Latin original Legenda maior, 1263
source: Google Books scan, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-12
note: The official Franciscan life of 1263; the scan has no OCR text layer.
annotation: Bonaventure's Legenda maior, the life the order made official in 1266 when it ordered the earlier lives destroyed: Francis's conversion, the rule, the stigmata at La Verna, the death and canonization, arranged by virtues rather than strict chronology. The Victorian translation by Lockhart with Manning's preface, in the same generation that rediscovered Francis for the English.

author: Antonio Attisani and Jane House
title: Franciscan Performance: A Theatre Lost and Found Again
journal: PAJ: A Journal of Performance and Art
publisher: PAJ: A Journal of Performance and Art 25.1 (Jan. 2003), 48-60, MIT Press; JSTOR 3246524
source: JSTOR, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-12
note: Francis and the early friars as performers; the jongleur de Dieu.
annotation: Attisani (translated by House) reads the early Franciscans as a performance practice: Francis as joculator Domini, the preaching in the piazza, the Greccio crib as staged Nativity, the body as the text, and argues that a theatre lost with the order's institutionalization can be recovered as a model for performance now.

author: Derrick de Kerckhove
title: Écriture, théâtre et neurologie
publisher: Études françaises 18.1 (printemps 1982), 109-128, issue 'Anatomie de l'écriture'; DOI 10.7202/036754ar
source: érudit open access, fetched by nodus1 2026-09-12 at Anthony's request
note: Fifth-century Athenian theatre as the institution that internalized the phonetic alphabet; McLuhan's student on tragedy and the brain. The 20-page version of the argument; the longer French one is 'Sur la fonction du théâtre comme agent d'intériorisation des effets de l'alphabet phonétique à Athènes au Ve siècle', in Duvignaud (ed.), Les Imaginaires II (10/18, 1979), pp. 345-368, not yet obtained; the English is 'A Theory of Greek Tragedy', SubStance 29 (1980/81), pp. 23-36.
annotation: De Kerckhove's thesis in its 1982 form: the Greek phonetic alphabet, by separating sound from meaning and forcing left-to-right sequential decoding, reorganized the brain's lateralization, and fifth-century tragedy was the public institution that trained an oral population in the new interiority, with the immobilized, speaking Prometheus as the emblematic case. Draws on Havelock, McLuhan, Innis and the split-brain neurology of the 1970s. A private English translation exists in private_notes (not in this repo).

author: Francesca Stavrakopoulou
title: The Jerusalem Tophet: Ideological Dispute and Religious Transformation
note: The tophet in Ben Hinnom as a Yahweh cult site rather than Molek's; child sacrifice in the Hebrew Bible.
annotation: Against the scholarly caricature of the tophet as a foreign Molek cult, Stavrakopoulou argues from the biblical texts themselves that the Ben Hinnom site was a Yahwistic sanctuary of child sacrifice whose later condemnation (Jeremiah, Kings) records an ideological dispute inside Judah's religion, not an import.

author: John Rundin
title: Pozo Moro, Child Sacrifice, and the Greek Legendary Tradition
source: ResearchGate copy, sent by Anthony over Telegram 2026-09-12
note: The Pozo Moro monument (Albacete) and the child-eating god; Phoenician sacrifice and Greek myth.
annotation: The relief on the Iberian funerary tower of Pozo Moro (c. 500 BCE, near Albacete) shows a two-headed monster on a throne receiving a bowl with a small human figure; Rundin reads it with the Phoenician tophet evidence and the Greek legends of child-devouring (Kronos, Tantalus, Lykaon) as one Mediterranean complex of sacrifice and its mythic memory.

author: Fernando Santos-Granero
title: The Enemy Within: Child Sorcery, Revolution, and the Evils of Modernization in Eastern Peru
booktitle: In Darkness and Secrecy: The Anthropology of Assault Sorcery and Witchcraft in Amazonia
editor: Whitehead, Neil L. and Wright, Robin
note: Child sorcery accusations among the Arawak peoples of the Selva Central.
annotation: Among the Ashaninka, Asheninka, Nomatsiguenga and Yanesha of the Selva Central, accusations of child sorcery, thought extinct since the 1970s, returned in the 1990s in the Shining Path years; Santos-Granero reads the child sorcerer as the figure through which a society under revolutionary violence and forced modernization names the enemy inside itself.
